bib.title: Linear Models for Classification (Chapter 4 of Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning)
bib.venue: Springer, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, ch. 4, pp. 179-224

question: How can classes be separated by linear decision surfaces, and how are the parameters fitted by discriminant functions, generative models, and discriminative (logistic) models, including a Bayesian treatment?
contributions: Develops generalized linear models for classification: discriminant functions (least squares, Fisher, perceptron), probabilistic generative models, probabilistic discriminative models (logistic, softmax, probit, IRLS, canonical links), the Laplace approximation, BIC and Bayesian logistic regression.

limits: Linear in fixed basis functions only; basis functions cannot adapt to data (p.205, deferred to later chapters).
Least squares is non-robust to outliers and ill suited to binary targets (Gaussian assumption fails), pp.185-186.
Perceptron gives no probabilistic outputs, does not generalise to K>2 and does not converge on non-separable data (p.196).
Laplace approximation is local, Gaussian, real-variable only and best with many data points (p.216); BIC assumes full-rank Hessian that often fails (p.217).
No empirical benchmark numbers; figures are synthetic illustrations.
Nonlinear transformations cannot remove class overlap (p.205). Chapter predates modern solvers (L-BFGS, SGD, regularised defaults) and calibration practice.
practices: Separate inference from decision: model p(Ck|x) then decide (p.180).
Prefer a single K-class discriminant with K linear functions over one-versus-rest or one-versus-one, which leave ambiguous regions (p.183).
Do not use least squares for classification when outliers or non-Gaussian targets matter; use logistic regression (pp.185-186).
Use logistic regression directly rather than generative Gaussians when M is large, since parameters grow linearly not quadratically (p.205).
Regularise or use a MAP prior in logistic regression when data are linearly separable (p.206).
Fit logistic regression with IRLS/Newton-Raphson; the cross-entropy is convex with a unique optimum (pp.207-208).
Pair softmax with multiclass cross-entropy, sigmoid with binary cross-entropy: gradient is (y-t)phi (p.209-210, canonical link).
Model label noise with a flip probability epsilon if mislabelling is expected (p.212).
Marginalising over w does not change decisions at equal priors but matters for complex decision criteria (p.220).

terms.definition: the class of models described by (4.3) are called generalized linear models: y(x)=f(w^T x + w0) with nonlinear activation f
In the machine learning literature f( · ) is known as an activation function, whereas its inverse is called a link function in the statistics literature.
K-1 classifiers each separating class Ck from not Ck
K(K-1)/2 binary discriminants, one per pair, majority vote
ratio of between-class variance to within-class variance J(w)=(m2-m1)^2/(s1^2+s2^2) = w^T S_B w / w^T S_W w
E_P(w) = -sum over misclassified n of w^T phi_n t_n
inverse of the logistic sigmoid, a = ln(sigma/(1-sigma)), the log odds ln[p(C1|x)/p(C2|x)]
p(Ck|x)=exp(ak)/sum_j exp(aj), multiclass generalisation of the logistic sigmoid
feature values are treated as independent, conditioned on the class Ck
E(w) = -ln p(t|w) = -sum {tn ln yn + (1-tn) ln(1-yn)}; multiclass (4.108)
iterative reweighted least squares: Newton-Raphson for logistic regression, w_new=(Phi^T R Phi)^-1 Phi^T R z with R_nn=y_n(1-y_n)
Phi(a) = integral of N(theta|0,1) up to a, the CDF of a standard Gaussian
choice f^-1(y)=psi(y) making the gradient of the NLL equal (1/s) sum (y_n - t_n) phi_n
Gaussian approximation q(z)=N(z|z0,A^-1) centred on a mode, A = -grad grad ln f at z0
the three terms M/2 ln 2pi - 1/2 ln|A| + ln p(theta_MAP) that penalise model complexity
Bayesian Information Criterion or Schwarz criterion: ln p(D|theta_MAP) - (1/2) M ln N
